### 2.10 Discussion

This methodological study provides insights for future vaccine allocation models that consider equity. These

are not specific to COVID-19 and could be applied to models for other epidemics, including but not limited to

pandemic influenza:

— Most modeling studies could show some results by subgroup, even if the focus of the paper is

not equity considerations. Indeed, most publications could easily show how the outcomes are distributed by

subgroups, instead of only showing total outcome in the population. This is especially true for COVID-19 models

that often have to include age categories due to the exponential increase in mortality rate with age: results by age

groups are already being generated and could easily be presented. As an example of how this can be done and how it

enhances the understanding of results, Chapman et al. show the distribution of vaccinations, as well as infections,

death and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) averted in each age group when the oldest age group (≥60 year

olds) is targeted for vaccination (after initial allocation to healthcare workers and long-term care facility residents)57.

— When modeling equity considerations in vaccine allocation, one should carefully choose the outcome

to be maximized. While most publications we found aimed at limiting some form of health burden (such as cases,

deaths, DALYs or years of life lost), some described the performance of each strategy in terms of doses allocated to

disadvantaged groups. Kipnis et al., for example, present total health outcome reduction of six different allocation

strategies, but present the results by subgroup (race/ethnicity and high neighbourhood deprivation index) in terms

of doses allocated59. An example of an alternative can be found in Hoover et al., where the impact of California’s

COVID-19 vaccine equity policy is shown on both vaccine administered and COVID-19 cases62. In some situations,

maximizing the number of vaccine doses given to a group does not necessarily maximize the number of lives saved

overall or in that group1. This underscores the importance of reporting both allocations and outcomes by group

and giving a rationale for what is being maximized. Additionally, the choice of health outcomes and how they

were collected (patient reporting, test result or physician assessment) can have consequences for equity68,69. This is

illustrated by Stafford et al., who show that minimizing different measures (here deaths or years of life lost) leads to

different disparities63.

— While it is preferable to stratify by multiple variables (as it is done by many publications57,59,60,63,50), some

models have considered vaccine allocation by only one variable56,1,61. When modeling vaccine allocation by one

variable only, the choice of the variable can have unexpected consequences for equity. This is, for example,

the case when comparing allocations by age groups and by race/ethnicity in the US. Indeed, as illustrated in one

34


<!-- Page 47 -->


case study1, those two variables are both associated with COVID-19 health outcomes (in the United States, older

individuals, as well as Hispanic, Black, Native and Pacific Islander have higher COVID-19 death rates), and negatively

associated with one another (in the United States, older individuals are disproportionately non-Hispanic White)

and therefore under a specific set of assumptions, basing an allocation on race/ethnicity could lead to more deaths

in each race/ethnicity stratum than basing it on age, even though race/ethnicity is very strongly associated with

mortality.

— The studies identified show diverse examples of how models can address equity considerations.

‘Equity’andrelatedconceptsmeandifferentthingstodifferentresearchers. Forexample,somepublicationsemphasize

equity as it relates specifically to the outcomes in the model and attempt to minimize inequality measures (which

may be relative60 or absolute56,59). Others note categories of preexisting disadvantage due to racism or geography,

for example, and focus on how to improve outcomes for already-disadvantaged groups58,61,63. A way to improve the

comparability of model predictions would be to present absolute outcomes (e.g. number of lives saved or lost) and

allocations (for example number of vaccines administered) by subgroup and overall, allowing a reader to calculate

disparity measures of particular interest, which may be relative or absolute, and may focus on particular subgroups

of the population. For example, Wrigley-Field et al. show on the same plots both the death rate in the population, as

well as the proportion of non-White people eligible for vaccination50.

— Data limitations can have implications for the questions being modeled. For example, the nine

publications that used data sources from the United States all included race/ethnicity in their model. As detailed

in table 2.1, the way race/ethnicity was coded varied widely between publications, with the number of race/ethnic

categories ranging from 258,63, 456,57,59,60,50, 61 up to 761. Additionally, some used single-race categories56,57,59,60,50,

while others included groups for individuals reporting two or more races1,61. While this is likely a result of data

limitations, modellers should be conscious that classification of race and ethnicity is a choice with implications for

equity and the inclusion of minorities70? ,71,72. Data limitations may impact outcome choice too, which, as described

above, can lead to different results.

— Care should be taken in model inputs that reflect already existing inequalities, such as life ex-

pectancy measures. The impact of a policy on life expectancy can be calculated using either population averages or

stratum-specific estimates of years of life left. For example, although life expectancy often varies by races/ethnicities73,

an average population-wide life expectancy is often used for all individuals of a given age in order to avoid down-

grading the value of saving the life of a person of a structurally disadvantaged racial/ethnic group1. Using the

average life expectancy may thus improve the number of vaccines allocated to people of structurally disadvantaged

35


<!-- Page 48 -->


race/ethnicities, but in doing so may reduce the total years of life saved. When considering age groups, however, it is

common to use age-specific life expectancy estimates, even if doing so downgrades the number of vaccines allocated

to older individuals to increase the total years of life saved. These opposite choices may or may not be justified, but

the fact that it is common to make opposite choices on these two demographic dimensions emphasizes that the

choice of which measure to use is an ethical one about how to balance efficiency and equity, rather than a purely

scientific one.

—MostCOVID-19vaccineallocationstudieswereconductedandpublishedinthefaceofsignificantuncertainty

about pathogen characteristics and transmission dynamics. Most of the papers we found57,58,59,63,50? dealt with

this by showing the robustness of their results across sensitivity analyses, thus strengthening the argument for the

allocation policies they identified as best. For example, Kadelka et al. replicated all their results varying scenarios

defined by three parameters of interest (ethnic homophily, relative contact level in high-contact versus low-contact

jobs, and relative proportion of people of colour compared to White people in high-contact jobs)58. In addition to

show robustness of results over parameters that may be uncertain or may change over time, it is important

to consider robustness over parameter distributions that may vary in different settings, such as age or

race/ethnicity. For example, Wrigley-Field et al. compare results in two US states (California and Minnesota) that

have different demographics50.

— Some of the papers considered only the direct protection from vaccination on those receiving it, not the

indirect effect on the rest of their communities57,1,50. Doing so can be tempting, as indirect effects may not happen

and can be more difficult to model with certainty, especially at the time allocation decisions are being made. Direct

protection of vaccination is always a useful metric and may be more robust to assumptions on vaccine protection

against infection or emergence of new variants. However, as highlighted by Jia et al., direct effects may not necessarily

represent a lower bound of overall effects of vaccination, for example, when vaccine wanes or when transmission or

fatality parameters increase over time, and should not be interpreted as such74.

### 3.11 Abstract

The protection against SARS-CoV-2 from a previous infection is difficult to estimate due to high rates of

vaccination and imperfect surveillance. Here, we estimate how infection-derived immunity protects against the

Omicron variant among unvaccinated individuals using a unique dataset from the Hutterite cohort study. Hutterites

are an Anabaptist religious group living in isolated communities of about a hundred people. We use a chain-binomial

model combining serological and virological surveillance data to estimate how infection-derived immunity protects

against Omicron infection. We find that antibody titers from prior infection are associated with a decrease in risk of

re-infection of up to 66% for the highest titer values. We also investigate the possible mechanism of protection and

find that a leaky model is the best fit, meaning that immune protection from prior infection is dependent on the

37


<!-- Page 50 -->


force of infection. We also investigate how pre-existing immunity impacts the infectiousness when reinfected and

find no statistical evidence of protection. These results help better understand how infection-derived immunity

works for COVID-19, particularly in the context of new variant emergence. The model can be used for future

epidemics and the parameters can inform model parametrization.

### 3.12 Introduction

The Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variant emerged in November 2021 and rapidly spread throughout the world,

becoming dominant in during spring 202275. This variant is characterized by numerous mutations that make it

less virulent and more transmissible compared to previously circulating variants76,77,78,79. By this time a significant

portion of the world population had some immune protection against SARS-CoV-2 from infection with previous

variants, vaccination, oramixofboth. Evaluatingtheprotectionconferredbyinfection-derivedimmunityspecifically

is complex due to antecedent infections that are often asymptomatic or unrecorded, and complex hybrid immunity

with a wide range of vaccine coverage and platforms used.

In this study we estimate how immune response from prior infection protects against the Omicron variant in a

unique unvaccinated population residing in Hutterite colonies in Canada. Previous publications have evaluated

the protection conferred by pre- Omicron infection-derived immunity against infection with the Omicron variant

among unvaccinated people or adjusting for vaccination status, and found 40% reduction in susceptibility80,81,82.

Relatively few studies have investigated how naturally-acquired antibody titers can serve as correlate of protection

from re-infection with Omicron83,84,85,86. We develop a method for estimating a dose-response relationship between

antibody titers and protection from reinfection using a chain-binomial model. This method also allows us to look at

the mechanism of protection from prior infection. In a leaky protection, the risk of infection scales with the density

or number of infectious contacts (making proportional protection from immunity less effective when there are

multiple opportunities to become infected), but does not for an all-or-nothing protection, where the people with

immunity are considered to be fully protected87,88. Previous consideration of this question has been limited to one

other study, which found evidence of a leaky protection89. Lastly, we also contribute to the limited literature90,91,89

on the impact of immunity from a prior infection on the infectiousness when re-infected.

We do this in the Hutterite Cohort Study, which poses a unique opportunity to study SARS-CoV-2 transmission

in unvaccinated populations. Hutterites are Anabaptists living in community structures of about 100 people called

colonies, who have been enrolled in frequent serology and virological surveillance for much of the COVID-19

pandemic. While they do not oppose all vaccination, they decided not to use mRNA vaccine technology and the vast

38


<!-- Page 51 -->


majority of the colony members are unvaccinated. Weekly virological testing allows for high quality characterization

of infections independently of symptoms, and close tight-knit structure of colonies makes the random mixing

assumption more tenable. Frequent serology testing, including immediately before the Omicron wave, allows for

characterization of immunity from previous infections. This density and quality of data is uncommon among

unvaccinated populations, especially during the Omicron variant wave when large proportions of the Canadian

population and other high-income countries had been vaccinated.

These estimates can help better understand immunity patterns and protection during the emergence of a new

variant, among unvaccinated populations, and can be useful for model parametrization.

### 3.13 Methods

### 3.14 Data source: Hutterite Cohort study

The Hutterite Cohort study enrolled a total of 1,849 participants across 21 Hutterite colonies in Alberta and

Saskatchewan, Canada, with an initial phase November 19, 2020, to June 4, 2021, and extension phases in July 11,

2021, to November 9, 2021; January 5, 2022, to July 24, 2022; February 2, 2023, to June 26, 2023. All individuals of

any age living on Hutterite colonies in Alberta and Saskatchewan that agreed to participate in the study by the start

date, November 19, 2020, were eligible, provided informed consent or assent for children was obtained. There were

no exclusion criteria.

Demographic information including age, sex, past medical history, medications, and vaccine history were

obtained at enrollment. Of 1,849 participants, 2% reported having received a COVID-19 vaccine. A self-collected

flocked nasal swab, a collection method previously validated and used extensively in the Hutterite community,

was collected at baseline from all participants. Nasal swabs were collected weekly from participants over the study

period, whether symptomatic or not. Serum was obtained for antibody testing at baseline and at the end of the study

period. Infection with SARS-CoV-2 was confirmed with real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), where

the amplification targets were the envelope gene and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase gene (limit of detection <

10 copies/reaction) on nasal samples collected weekly. IgG antibody titers (using recombinant SARS-CoV-2 spike

RBD) were obtained from serum samples collected at the beginning, middle and end of each study phase.

The protocol was approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board, the ethics review board at the

University of Calgary, and the ethics review board at the University of Saskatchewan. Participants gave written

39


<!-- Page 52 -->


informed consent. Participants provided consent for children, and assent was also directly sought from children

aged 7 to 15 years.

### 3.15 Data coding

We focus our analysis on the study phase from January to July 2022 which coincides with the rise in infections

with the Omicron variant in Canada. Firstly, based on weekly PCR testing against SARS-CoV-2 between January

2022 and May 2022, each week we define participants as infected and infectious (I) the first time they test positive,

and susceptible (S) otherwise. Secondly, we use serological testing in January 2022 as indicator of immunity from

prior infection.

We restrict our analysis to study participants for whom we have serology results at the beginning of the phase.

As participants are considered not to have been infected on weeks without test results, we restrict the analysis to the

study participants that test regularly, defined as 10 tests or more during the phase. Furthermore, as participants build

an immune response after getting infected with the Omicron variant, we censor them after they become infected.

We include them as part of the category with high antibody titer in a sensitivity analysis in Appendix 3.25. As these

restrictions lead to small sample sizes in some colonies, we exclusively run our analysis in colony-weeks where >50%

non-previously infected participants test. We vary this cutoff from 30% - 70% in a sensitivity analysis in Appendix

3.24.

3.15.1 Notation

We count in each colony-week the number of individuals in the following categories:

• S0 t−1: the number of susceptible individuals with antibody titers under a threshold (type 0) at time t −1, potential infectees for time t.

• S1 t−1: the number of susceptible individuals with antibody titers above a threshold (type 1) at time t −1, potential infectees for time t.

• I0 t−1: the number of newly infected individuals of type 0 at time t −1, potential infectors for time t.

• I1 t−1: the number of newly infected individuals of type 1 at time t −1, potential infectors for time t.

• I0 t : the number of newly infected individuals of type 0 at time t.

• I1 t : the number of newly infected individuals of type 1 at time t.

• SX t−1: the number of susceptible individuals with titer X at time t −1, potential infectees for time t.

• IX t : the number of newly infected individuals with titer X at time t.

### 3.19 Discussion

We use a rich and unique dataset of residents of Hutterite colonies that were followed intensely in 2022 during

the rise of Omicron in Canada to provide insight into the strength and mechanism of immune protection derived

through COVID-19 infection. The quantity of surveillance data is unmatched in a completely unvaccinated pop-

ulation, with most participants adhering extremely well to weekly PCR testing, which is done independently of

symptoms. This allows us to have probably very limited under-reporting or reporting bias. In addition, this study

had collected serology before the spread of Omicron, allowing for evaluation of immunity from prior infection.

This is not dependent on previous infection having been symptomatic or recorded, and focusing on titer values

allows to not have to make assumptions on timing of infection or waning.

We found that people with antibodies from prior infection had a 31% reduction in susceptibility (0R: 0.69

(95% CI : 0.53; 0.91)). This is consistent with the other studies that have evaluated the protection conferred by

pre-Omicron infection-derived immunity against re-infection with Omicron variant, among unvaccinated people.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 studies, Stein et al. found that among unvaccinated people, protection

from past infection against re-infection with Omicron was 45.3% (95% CI: 17.3-76.1%)80. In another meta-analysis,

Bobrovitz et al. found that previous infection protects against Omicron infection by 69.5% (52.9-75.9%) at 3 months,

which drops to 24.7% (16.4-35.5%) by 12 months (10 studies)81. In a third meta-analysis using 5 studies, Hu et al.

calculated a pooled incidence rate ratio for naturally acquired antibodies against reinfection with Omicron variant

of 0.61 (0.42-0.87)82.

Considering a dose-response relationship, we found that antibody titers are associated with a decrease in the risk

of infection, with a 40% decrease in risk for medium antibody titers (the threshold we use for the binary analysis) and

up to 66% for the highest titers. Few other studies have investigated how antibody titers from pre-Omicron infection

can serve as correlate of protection from re-infection with Omicron variant, among unvaccinated people. Perez-Saez

et al. showed that the hazard ratio for Omicron infection seems to decrease with total antibodies (IgG/A/M) against

the receptor binding domain of spike protein, without being statistically significant83. Zambrana et al. found that

titers in spike-binding assay were not associated with Omicron infection, but were protective against symptomatic

49


<!-- Page 62 -->


infection, adjusting for prior vaccination and prior infection, in a population that is 32% unvaccinated85. Hollister

et al. measured antibody binding to both receptor binding domain (RBD) and S2 subunit domain (S2) of the spike

protein. They found that among unvaccinated individuals, each three-fold increase in RBD and S2 titer value was

estimated to reduce the odds of reinfection by 23% (0.65, 0.92) and 18% (0.64, 1.04), respectively86.

We have found that the leaky model was the best fit, meaning that immune protection from prior infection is

dependent on the force of infection. This is consistent with the only other study that looked at this question. In

Connecticut correctional facilities, Lind et al. found that protection from prior infection was lower when contact

was closer, suggesting that the protection may be leaky89. This result confirms that interventions to limit the intensity

of contacts can help limit transmission, even with the emergence of a very transmissible and immune-escaping

variant like Omicron.

We did not find people with immunity from prior infections to be significantly less infectious (OR: 0.88 (95%

CI: 0.57; 1.39)). This could be due to small effect size or data limitation. This result is consistent with three other

studies that have investigated how infection-derived immunity impacts infectiousness, which have found variable

results, with small or non-significant reductions.

Among contacts in California state prisons, Tan et al. estimated that prior infection reduced an unvaccinated index

case’s risk of transmitting by 23% (95% CI: 3–39%)90. Using contact tracing data from Geneva Switzerland, Mongin

et al. estimated that previous infection in the index case reduced the secondary attack rate (SAR) during the Omicron

wave by 4.3% (95% CI: 1.3-7.3%)91. Lastly, using surveillance data from residents of Connecticut correctional facilities

during the Omicron period, Lind et al. found that the prior infection status of the index case was associated with a

non-significantly lower hazard of SARS-CoV-2 transmission following close contact at the cellblock level (HR: 0.52

(95% CI: 0.27–1.03)) and cell level (HR: 0.72 (95% CI: 0.25–2.03))89.

Our work is subject to several limitations. Firstly, while we have weekly testing data from January to July

2022, our restriction on the percentage of people needing to test for a given colony-week to be included in the

analysis results in us using only a portion of the data. Most of the colony-weeks contributing to the analysis are in

January-March, and only one colony (269) contributes data in April. The duration of follow-up is limited and we do

not consider longer-term protection. Secondly as we do not always know when participants were initially infected,

we only use antibody titer values and not timing of infection. Thirdly, as we restrict our dataset to the people that

participated in serology testing in January 2022, and then further restrict to people very frequently testing by PCR,

we only have data on a portion of each of the colony and assume that they are exchangeable with people not testing.

50


<!-- Page 63 -->


We show in Appendix section 3.22 that the adults included in our analysis do not differ by age or gender from the

rest of the adult population.

Limitations are also caused by our modeling approach, which relies on several simplifying assumptions. First,

the use of Binomials assumes that each participant comes into contact with every other colony member. This

assumption may be reasonable, especially for aerosol contact, as in Hutterite communities residents work and share

meals together, the children under 15 years old attend school together, and everyone gathers for daily church service.

Second, in the binary analysis, grouping people into two categories based on antibody titers is a drastic simplification.

However, we test a range of thresholds between the two groups and then model a more complicated and realistic

dose-response relationship. Third, both of the dose-response models assume that the log odds of infection vary

linearly with titer dilutions. We verify the validity of the assumption in a sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 3.26.

Fourth, we only consider individuals to be in the infected and infectious category for one week, on the first week

they test positive, and even if they keep testing positive the following week (8% do). This is a necessary assumption

as people can keep testing positive by PCR and no longer be infectious. We do not consider variation in duration of

infectiousness as we do not have any data that could inform this parameter.

The methods we propose here could be applied to future epidemics or variant emergence with serology and

virological testing available.

## 4

## Conclusion

In these three chapters, I have used mathematical modeling to better understand the immune response to

SARS-Cov-2, and to evaluate and compare vaccine allocation policies, with a specific attention to including equity

in models. While the picture of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has changed since some of these analyses were initially

published, or when the data for Chapter 3 was collected in Hutterite colonies, these chapters illustrate how powerful

of a tool modeling can be. The lessons for equity in modeling from Chapter 2 and the methods to estimate natural

immunity combining serological and virological data from Chapter 3 are specifically aimed to be used to help future

models for epidemics to come.

In Chapter 1 I showed that, once health-care workers and people older than 75 are vaccinated, prioritizing

allocation of COVID-19 vaccines for 65-74 year olds saves both more lives and more years of life in each racial/ethnic

group than prioritizing front-line workers, in the United States as a whole and in nearly every state. In Chapter 2, I

highlight that only few vaccine allocation models took equity into account and I provide examples of how modeling

can be used to answer equity-related questions. I also argue that future vaccine allocation models should take equity

considerations into account and highlight advice for how to do so. In Chapter 3, I estimate how infection-derived

immunity protects against Omicron infection. I find that antibody titers from antecedent infection are associated

52


<!-- Page 65 -->


with a decrease in the risk of re-infection of up to 66% for the highest antibody titer values. I also investigate the

possible mechanism of protection and find that a leaky model fits the data best, which suggests that the immune

protection from prior infection is dependent on the force of infection.

# Equity considerations in COVID-19 vaccine allocation modelling: a literature review

**Authors:** Eva Rumpler Marc Lipsitch

## 1 Abstract

We conducted a literature review of COVID-19 vaccine allocation modelling papers, specifically looking for publications that considered equity. We found that most models did not take equity into account, with the vast majority of publications presenting aggregated results and no results by any subgroup (e.g. age, race, geography, etc). We then give examples of how modelling can be useful to answer equity questions, and highlight some of the findings from the publications that did. Lastly, we describe seven considerations that seem important to consider when including equity in future vaccine allocation models.

## 2 Introduction

As COVID-19 vaccines became available in 2021, countries and regions around the globe had to define criteria for prioritizing access to vaccines. For example, WHO’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) released a roadmap in October 2020 for prioritizing uses of COVID-19 vaccines in the context of limited supply. In situations of community transmission, they recommended vaccines be first given to healthcare workers and older individuals, followed by groups (defined by health states or sociodemographic status) at significantly higher risk of severe disease and deaths [1]. Similarly in the US, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommended vaccines be allocated first to health care personnel and residents of long-term care facilities, followed by older individuals, people with high-risk medical conditions, and essential workers not already included [2].

Some have argued that vaccine allocation should provide equitable protection of individuals and should aim to reduce (or at least not further increase) inequities in health burden. For example, WHO’s SAGE developed a values framework for the allocation and prioritization of COVID-19 vaccines, defining six core principles for equitable protection. In addition to human well-being, equal respect, reciprocity and legitimacy, two of the principles were global equity (i.e. vaccine access to all counties, particularly low- and middle-income countries) and national equity (i.e. preferential allocation for vulnerable groups and groups experiencing higher burden) [3]. Similarly, the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, in its 2020 Framework for equitable allocation of COVID-19 vaccine defined three ethical principles: maximum benefit, equal concern, and mitigation of health inequities, defined as the obligation to explicitly address the higher burden of COVID-19 experienced by some populations [4].

Modelling has provided useful contributions to identifying the best performing allocation strategies for COVID-19 vaccines and has helped inform policy making in the face of uncertainty about the vaccines and pathogens characteristics. Many publications have modelled the performance of different allocation strategies, often comparing transmission-minimizing approaches targeting younger adults with mortality-minimizing approaches targeting older age groups when vaccine stock is limited [5, 6, 7, 8].

Despite huge inequities in disease burden distribution and large modelling literature on allocation optimization, however, few publications modelled equity considerations. Here we present a literature review conducted to identify publications that did look at equity and COVID-19 allocation modelling. We highlight some of their main findings and summarize advice to modellers wanting to include equity in future models.

## 3 Methods

We conducted a literature review and expert-opinion elicitation in search of papers that looked at COVID-19 vaccine allocation, presenting outcomes stratified by any characteristic (age, race, ethnicity, occupation, geography, etc).

We performed a literature review using PubMed, including studies published between 2019 and May 2024. We included all peer-reviewed publications and pre-prints that were relevant to our search terms for:

- • COVID-19 : ”COVID-19 Vaccines”[MeSH] OR ”SARS-CoV*”[ti] OR COVID*[ti] OR coronavir*[ti] OR NCOV[ti]

- • Vaccine: vaccine*[ti] OR vaccination[ti]

- • Modelling: ”Computer Simulation”[Mesh] OR ”Epidemiological Models”[Mesh] OR ”Models, Statistical”[Mesh] OR model*[ti] OR scenario[ti] OR strategies[ti] OR strategy[ti] OR prioritization[ti]

- • Disparity or subpopulation: ”Demography”[Majr] OR ”Population Groups, US”[Mesh] OR ”Age Factors”[Mesh] OR ”Race Factors”[Mesh] OR ”Aged”[Mesh] OR demographic*[ti] OR equit*[tiab] OR inequit*[tiab] OR ”fair distribution”[tiab: 3] OR ”fair allocation”[tiab: 3] OR race[ti] OR racial*[ti] OR ethnic*[ti] OR age[ti] OR aged[ti] OR elder*[ti] OR ”risk factor*”[ti]

From this search, we identified 251 papers to be reviewed. After review, 6 of them corresponded to our criterion for inclusion.

To look for additional relevant studies, we carried out a manual search of all studies cited or citing the papers we had already identified and found an additional 6 publications.

Finally, having found only a limited number of research papers that meet our criteria in the literature review, we conducted an expert-opinion elicitation to identify research papers that we may have missed. We contacted four experts in public health and the study of disparities, asking if they knew of publications matching our criteria. All provided publications we had identified already. The experts were (in alphabetical order) Dr. Mary Bassett (MD, MPH), Harvard University, Dr. Mathew Kiang (MPH, ScD), Stanford University, Dr. Andrew C. Stokes (MA, PhD), Boston University, and Dr. Elizabeth Wrigley-Field (MA, PhD), University of Minnesota.

Our literature review has limitations. Firstly, although we searched for the most publications possible by doing both a literature review and expert-opinion elicitation, there may be publications that we missed. It can be especially difficult to identify publications as not all explicitly mention equity, and some use diverse vocabulary to describe similar analyses. Secondly, we focused our literature review on prioritization of COVID-19 initial vaccination. We did not include publications regarding allocation of boosters as these took place under less vaccine quantity constraints.

## 4 Literature review findings

Of the numerous publications that modelled COVID-19 vaccine allocation, most did not explicitly consider equity. Despite an extended literature search directed at literature considering equity between population subgroups and manual review of 251 publications, only 6 (2.4%) [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14] were COVID-19 vaccine allocation modelling studies presenting results by some sub-group. From manual search among studies cited or citing those studies, we identified an additional 6 publications [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Expert-opinion elicitation of four experts did not provide any additional publications. Of these, 11 explicitly consider equity in their model, and one [10] strives to identify the optimal allocation without explicitly mentioning equity. Characteristics and key findings from these 12 publications can be found in Table 1 below.

Contrary to the hypothesis of an equity/efficiency trade-off, there often is no such trade-off found, or it is weaker than one might expect, as it can be possible to minimize total deaths or infections while simultaneously reducing disparities between groups in the risks of these outcomes. Multiple publications have found that the most efficient policy overall is either the one most beneficial to disadvantaged groups, or one that prioritizes disadvantaged groups [15, 14, 18, 11, 13, 17]. Notably, Chen et al. (2022) show that prioritizing the most disadvantaged based on any criteria (age, race/ethnicity, occupation, or income) increases both equity (which they define as mitigation of mortality disparities in disadvantaged demographic group) and social utility (which they define as minimizing mortality in the entire population) [15]. Rumpler et al. (2023) show that a vaccine allocation policy targeting older individuals saves most lives overall and among every racial/ethnic group despite leading to less vaccines allocated to non-White people than an allocation policy targeting non-healthcare front-line workers [14]. Wrigley-Field et al. (2021) show that targeting racial/ethnic groups (or geography) makes vaccine available to people with higher mortality rates, and also increases the proportion of BIPOC eligible [18]. Kadelka et al. (2022) show that taking race/ethnicity into account when prioritizing vaccines may reduce the total number of deaths, especially when also assuming that proportionately more people of color occupy high-contact jobs [11]. Rosenstrom et al. (2022) show that a strategy to increase vaccination uptake in non-White individuals reduces deaths overall without significantly increasing the infection rate [13]. Stafford et al. (2023) find that to minimize disease burden (death), the age cutoff for vaccine eligibility should be younger for people of color than for White people, suggesting that universal age thresholds aren’t the most efficient [17]. While there are numerous instances of policies that improve equity and efficiency simultaneously compared to alternatives, we note that definitions of equity can vary and that maximizing one aspect may not maximize all. We discuss this further below.

Researchers face trade-offs in formulating research questions and performing the analyses to answer these questions A first trade-off is between considering allocation policies that are complex and may be optimal, versus considering simpler policies that may be more realistic. Some publications looked at allocation rules that consider only one or two characteristics (e.g. race, age, occupation, etc) [14, 9, 18, 12, 13, 17, 19, 20, 16], whereas other studies looked for the one optimal policy over multiple stratifying variables. These usually performs better but may be more difficult to implement due to a high number of variables used to define allocation priority, and may not be generalizable to other populations with different joint distributions of predictors and outcomes [10, 11, 15]. While considering finer allocation rules that can vary over multiple variables can lead to more efficient allocations, as shown by Kadelka at al. (20222), increasing the number of levels within each parameters can too, lead to better performance [11]. A second trade-off may exist between political acceptability and equity. Indeed while some publications consider vaccine allocation by race/ethnicity categories directly [11, 13, 17, 15], others like Wrigley-Field et al. (2021) propose using geography-based vaccine allocation at the census-tract level as an alternative to race/ethnicity strategies [18]. Multiple other papers [10, 19, 20] consider geographical units at various levels (county, states, country, etc) as targets for vaccination.

Overall, comparing results from these 12 publications is made difficult by the fact that they use different terms and vocabulary, sometimes without clear definitions. This may in part be due to the fact that they come from different literatures, for example the two publications from decision science journals [19, 20] contrast with some of the infectious disease modelling ones [11, 13, 17, 15].

## 5 Discussion

The publications [14, 18, 10, 9, 11, 12, 13, 17, 19, 20, 15, 16] we have identified provide some insights to take into account when including equity in vaccine allocation modelling:

- • Most modelling studies could show some results by subgroup, even if the focus of the paper is not equity considerations. Indeed, most publications could easily show how the outcomes are distributed by subgroups, instead of only showing total outcome in the population. This is especially true for COVID-19 models that often have to include age categories due to the exponential increase in mortality rate: results by age groups are already being generated and could easily be presented. As an example of how this can be done and how it enhances the understanding of results, Chapman et al. (2022) show the distribution of vaccinations, as well as infections, death and DALYs averted in each age group when the oldest age groups ( $\geq$ 60 year olds) is targeted for vaccination (after initial allocation to healthcare workers and long-term care facility residents) [10].

- • When modelling equity considerations in vaccine allocation, one should carefully choose the outcome to be maximized. While most publications we found aimed at limiting some form of health burden (such as cases, deaths, DALYs or years of life lost), some described the performance of each strategy in terms of doses allocated to disadvantaged groups. Kipnis et al. (2021) for example present total health outcome reduction of six different allocation strategies, but presents the results by subgroup (race/ethnicity and high neighborhood deprivation index) in terms of doses allocated [12]. An example of an alternative can be found in Hoover et al. (2024), where the impact of California’s COVID-19 vaccine equity policy is shown on both vaccine administered and COVID-19 cases [16]. In some situations, maximizing the number of vaccine doses given to a group does not necessarily maximize the number of lives saved overall or in that group [14]. The possibility of such an outcome underscores the importance of reporting both allocations and outcomes by group and giving a rationale for what is being maximized.

- • Another aspect to take into account in setting up a modelling study for vaccine allocation is choosing which subgroup to be maximized over. In a situation where there are two predictors of the outcome that are negatively correlated to one another, maximizing the outcome over the weaker of the two predictors can lead to making the wrong allocation in terms of total outcome. This is for example likely to be the case when comparing allocations by age groups and by race/ethnicity in the US. Indeed, as illustrated in the case study [14], those two variables are both predictors of the outcome (in the US, older individuals, as well as Hispanic, Black, Native and Pacific Islander have higher COVID-19 death rates), and negatively correlated to one another (in the US, older individuals are disproportionately non-Hispanic White) and therefore under a specific set of assumptions, basing an allocation on race/ethnicity could lead to more deaths in each race/ethnicity stratum than basing it on age, even though race/ethnicity is a very strong predictor of mortality. A solution to avoid this issue is to maximize the outcome over the strongest predictor (age in this example), or ideally, to stratify by multiple predictors, as done by others [10, 18, 12, 13, 17].

- • The studies identified show diverse examples of how models can address equity considerations. ”Equity” and related concepts mean different things to different researchers. For example, some publications emphasize equity as it relates specifically to the outcomes in the model and attempt to minimize inequality measures (which may be relative [13] or absolute [9, 12]. Others note categories of preexisting disadvantage due to racism or geography, for example, and focus on how to improve outcomes for already-disadvantaged groups [11, 15, 17]. A way to improve the comparability of model predictions would be to present absolute outcomes (number of lives saved or lost, for example) and allocations (number of vaccines administered, for example) by subgroup, allowing a reader to calculate disparity measures of particular interest, which may be relative or absolute, and may focus on particular subgroups of the population. To facilitate interpretation by different readers according to multiple conceptions of equity, it may be advisable to present absolute outcomes (e.g., cases, deaths) overall and in each group, rather than or in addition to presenting results on the differences between groups. For example, Wrigley-Field et al. (2021) show on the same plots both the death rate in the population, as well as the proportion of BIPOC eligible for vaccination [18].

- • Care should be taken in model input not to include measures that reflect already existing inequalities. For example, although life expectancy may vary by races/ethnicities [21], an average life expectancy should be used for all individuals of a given age in order to avoid downgrading the value of saving a life of a person of a certain age in already disadvantaged group [14].

- • Most COVID-19 vaccine allocation studies were conducted and published in the face of significant uncertainty about pathogen characteristics and transmission dynamics. Most of the papers we found [18, 10, 11, 12, 17, 20] dealt with this by showing the robustness of their results across sensitivity analyses, thus strengthening the argument for the allocation policies they identified as best. For example, Kadelka et al. (2022), replicated all their results varying scenarios defined by three parameters of interest (ethnic homophily, relative contact level in high- vs low-contact jobs, and relative proportion of people of color compared to White people in high-contact jobs) [11].

- • Some of the papers considered only the direct protection from vaccination on those receiving it, not the indirect effect on the rest of their communities [14, 18, 10]. Doing so can be tempting, as indirect effects may not happen and can be more difficult to model with certainty, especially at the time allocation decisions are being made. Direct protection of vaccination is always a useful metric and may be more robust to assumptions on vaccine protection against infection or emergence of new variants. However, as highlighted by Jia et al. (2024), direct effects may not necessarily represent a lower bound of overall effects of vaccination, for example when vaccine wanes or when transmission or fatality parameters increase over time [22].

We thank Carrie Wade from Countway Library, Harvard Medical School for her help in refining the Pubmed search. We thank the four experts that answered our expert-opinion elicitation.
